presentation: Is it possible to learn a language in a month?
No, it's impossible — but it's possible to learn the basics.
Did you understand the lecture?
I misunderstood one part, so I re-read my notes.
Is your school international?
Yes, it's multicultural — students from six countries.
Are some students underpaid after graduation?
Yes, many graduates are underpaid and overworked.
Is the exam schedule regular?
No, it's irregular this term.
Do you agree that homework is useless?
I disagree — but overloading students is unhelpful.
Is the library automatic?
Yes, the doors are automatic and the system is semi-digital.
Are you bilingual?
I'm bilingual now and I'm becoming trilingual.
Is cheating illegal at university?
It's not illegal, but it's unacceptable.
What does "empower" mean?
To give power: education empowers people.

reading.title: Abdurauf Fitrat — the man who rewrote Uzbek education
text: Abdurauf Fitrat was born in 1886 in Bukhara, then an independent emirate with an unreformed, medieval education system. Boys memorised Arabic texts for years without understanding them; girls were mostly uneducated. Fitrat studied at a madrasa, but he was dissatisfied. In 1909 he went to Istanbul, where he saw modern, multilingual schools, and he returned with an unpopular idea: Bukhara had to rethink everything.

He became the leading thinker of the Jadids — the "new-method" reformers. In his books he wrote that a nation with an illiterate population could never be independent. He designed a new curriculum, wrote textbooks and dictionaries, and co-founded schools where children learned science, geography and languages instead of rote learning. When the emir's government misunderstood him as a revolutionary and threatened him, he continued from Tashkent.

In the 1920s Fitrat was, for a short time, the minister of education of the Bukhara republic. He reorganised the university, sent students abroad on scholarships to Germany and wrote plays, poems and the first serious works on Uzbek music and literature. His interdisciplinary mind moved between linguistics, history, drama and politics.

In 1937, during the repression, Fitrat was arrested and in October 1938 he was shot — together with Qodiriy and Cho'lpon. His books were banned for fifty years. He was rehabilitated in 1956, and today his name is on the Institute of Uzbek Language and Literature. Unprecedented for his time, his idea is now obvious: education is the precondition of independence.

intro: Suffiks — so'z OXIRIga qo'shiladi va TURKUMNI o'zgartiradi: happy (sifat) → happiness (ot) → happily (ravish).

OT: -ness (happiness), -ment (development), -tion/-sion (creation, decision), -ity (activity), -ship (friendship), -hood (childhood), -ance/-ence (importance, silence); ODAM: -er/-or (teacher, actor), -ist (artist, environmentalist).
SIFAT: -able/-ible (readable), -ful (beautiful), -less (hopeless), -ous (dangerous), -al (natural), -ic (poetic), -y (snowy), -ed/-ing (finished, running).
RAVISH: -ly (quickly, environmentally); FE'L: -en (widen, strengthen).

presentation: What is the biggest environmental problem?
Pollution — and the carelessness of polluters.
Is plastic harmful?
Yes, it's harmful and hopelessly slow to break down.
What is sustainability?
Sustainability is the ability to continue without harming the future.
Is DiCaprio an actor or an activist?
He's an actor and an environmentalist.
Is the river drinkable?
No, it's undrinkable — dangerously polluted.
How can we strengthen environmental laws?
By toughening penalties and widening protected areas.
Is deforestation reversible?
Partly — reforestation is possible but slow.
Are electric cars environmentally friendly?
Environmentally, yes — but their production is energy-intensive.
What is your government's commitment?
A commitment to carbon neutrality by 2050.
Is the situation hopeless?
Not hopeless, but worrying.
notes: Imlo: happy → happiness (y → i); create → creation (e tushadi); big → bigger (undosh ikkilanadi).
-ful faqat bitta l: beautiful, careful; -fully: carefully.
-ic / -ical: historic (tarixiy ahamiyatli) / historical (tarixga oid); economic / economical.

reading.title: Leonardo DiCaprio — the actor whose foundation protects the planet
text: Leonardo DiCaprio was born in 1974 in Los Angeles. His acting career started early: at 19 he received his first Oscar nomination, and "Titanic" (1997) made him globally famous. But his success as an actor is only half of the story. In 1998, at 24, he created the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation, an organisation whose mission is the protection of wildlife and the environment.

His environmentalism is practical and measurable. The foundation has given more than 100 million dollars to conservation projects: the preservation of rainforests, the protection of endangered tigers and sharks, and the creation of marine reserves. His documentaries — "The 11th Hour" (2007) and "Before the Flood" (2016) — are watched by millions and are used in schools to raise awareness of climate change. In 2014 the United Nations named him Messenger of Peace for climate issues.

DiCaprio is realistic about his own carelessness: he flies a lot, and his carbon footprint is enormous. Critics call this hypocritical; he calls it a reason to give more. He has also invested in sustainable businesses — electric cars, plant-based food and reusable products — because, he says, "activism without economics is hopeless."

When he finally won his Oscar in 2016 for "The Revenant", his speech was not about acting. It was about global warming: "Climate change is real, it is happening right now. It is the most urgent threat facing our entire species." Uzbek students who admire him usually know the actor; the environmentalist is worth knowing too.

lessons.vocab_topic: Essential Words 3 — Technology and innovation (texnologiya va innovatsiya)

objectives: ought to (maslahat, rasmiy should) ni tasdiq, inkor va savolda tuzish.
be able to ni can o'rniga barcha zamonlarda ishlatish (will be able to, have been able to, was able to).
could vs was able to (umumiy qobiliyat vs aniq holatda uddalash) farqi.

materials: Essential Words 3 — Technology and innovation (texnologiya va innovatsiya) CORE 20 varag'i.
timeline: Ustoz: "You should study. You ought to study. You must study. You have to study." — kuch shkalasi. Keyin: "I can code. I was able to code at 12. I will be able to code in Python by June." — can'ning zamonlari.
20 savol, 15 soniya; oldingi dars lug'ati + grammatikasi.

Kitob jadvallari: OUGHT TO + V1 (= should, rasmiyroq): darak / ought not to / Ought I to…?; BE ABLE TO + V1 (= can, lekin barcha zamonlarda: am/is/are/was/were/will be/have been able to). Modal takrori: must/have to/should/ought to/can/could/be able to/may/might — ma'no va zamon jadvali.
Essential Words 3 — Technology and innovation (texnologiya va innovatsiya) — CORE 20
Har so'z bilan yangi grammatika qolipida gap.
Kitob: formula → gap → tarjima; warm-up / normativ / coin me'yorlari.
Sinf matni + 3 topshiriq; kitob Topic'lari uyga.
Ko'p uchragan xatolar doskada; STRONG lug'at kuchlilarga.

intro: OUGHT TO + V1 — "kerak, to'g'ri bo'ladi" (should bilan bir xil, rasmiyroq): "You ought to study harder." Inkor: ought not to (oughtn't to); savol: "Ought I to call her?" (kam; odatda Should I…?).

BE ABLE TO + V1 — "qila olmoq" — can'ning barcha zamonlardagi shakli: "She is able to swim" (= can), "They weren't able to come" (= couldn't), "I will be able to help" (can'ning kelajagi yo'q!), "I have been able to finish" (perfect).
could — o'tgandagi umumiy qobiliyat ("I could swim at five"); was able to — bitta aniq holatda uddaladi ("I was able to escape").
Modal xaritasi: majburiyat — must/have to; maslahat — should/ought to; qobiliyat — can/be able to; ruxsat — can/may; ehtimol — may/might/could.
formulas: You ought not to be rude.
Ought I to call her now?
S + am/is/are/was/were/will be + able to + V1
She is able to swim well. / I will be able to code by June.
U yaxshi suza oladi. / Iyungacha dasturlay olaman.
S + be + not + able to / Be + S + able to…?
They aren't able to come today. / Are you able to help me?
Ular bugun kela olmaydi. / Menga yordam bera olasanmi?
Perfect / could vs was able to
have/has been able to; could (umumiy) — was able to (aniq holat)
I have been able to finish. / He could read at four; he was able to fix the bug yesterday.
Tugatishga muvaffaq bo'ldim. / U to'rt yoshida o'qiy olardi; kecha xatoni tuzata oldi.
presentation: Ought I to buy a new laptop?
You ought to wait — the new model is due in May.
Were you able to fix the connection?
Yes, I was able to fix it after an hour.
Will AI be able to replace teachers?
It will be able to help, but it won't be able to replace them.
Ought companies to collect our data?
They ought not to collect more than they need.
Has technology been able to make people more social?
It has been able to connect us, but not always to make us closer.
Could Bill Gates code as a teenager?
Yes, he could code at 13, and at 20 he was able to write an operating system.
Are you able to work without your phone?
Honestly, I'm not able to concentrate without it — and I ought to change that.
Ought children to have smartphones?
They ought not to have one before twelve, in my view.
Will you be able to finish the essay tonight?
I'll be able to finish the plan, not the essay.
Should we ban social media in schools, or ought we to teach digital literacy?
We ought to teach digital literacy.
notes: ought to dan keyin doim to: "ought to go" ("ought go" — xato); should dan keyin to yo'q.
can — faqat Present; could — Past/muloyim; qolgan zamonlar — be able to.
"managed to" = was able to (aniq holatda uddaladi).
Essential Words 3: innovation, digital literacy, connectivity, social isolation, screen time, breakthrough, obsolete, user-friendly, cyberbullying.
mistakes: I will be able to help you.

She could swim when she was five.

I was able to escape the fire yesterday.

reading.title: Bill Gates — the man who was able to put a computer on every desk
text: Bill Gates was born in 1955 in Seattle. At 13 he was able to use a computer at school — an enormous machine that few schools had — and he ought to have been doing his homework, but instead he was writing programs. At 20 he dropped out of Harvard because he believed something that sounded impossible: that one day there would be a personal computer on every desk and in every home.

In 1975 he and Paul Allen founded Microsoft. Gates was able to see what others couldn't: hardware would become cheap, so the money was in software. He licensed the operating system MS-DOS to IBM instead of selling it — a decision that made Microsoft the most valuable company in the world by the 1990s. Windows and Office were soon on almost every computer on the planet.

Not everyone admired him. Courts ruled that Microsoft had acted as a monopoly, and critics said its products were not user-friendly. But nobody was able to deny his influence: the digital age ran on his software.

In 2000 Gates did something few billionaires have been able to do — he gave most of his fortune away. The Gates Foundation has spent more than 70 billion dollars on vaccines, clean water and education, and it has been able to help eradicate polio from almost every country. "Technology," he says, "is just a tool. People ought to use it to make lives better — that is the only measure that matters."

intro: BE GOING TO + V1 — oldindan reja yoki dalilli bashorat: "It's going to rain soon." / "I'm going to apply."
PRESENT CONTINUOUS — kelishilgan, belgilangan reja: "We're meeting them at 6 p.m."
PRESENT SIMPLE — jadval (transport, dars, ochilish): "The train leaves at 9 a.m."
BE ABOUT TO — juda yaqin: "She is about to leave." BE DUE TO — belgilangan vaqt: "The meeting is due to start at 10."
BE TO + V1 — rasmiy reja/buyruq (yangiliklar): "The President is to visit tomorrow."
BE BOUND/SURE/CERTAIN TO — yuqori ishonch: "He is bound to succeed." BE LIKELY/UNLIKELY TO — ehtimol: "They are likely to win."
formulas: It's going to rain soon. / I'm going to apply for the job.
Tez orada yomg'ir yog'adi. / Ishga ariza beraman (rejam).
Biz ular bilan soat 6 da uchrashamiz.
be about to / be due to
S + be about to + V1 / S + be due to + V1
She is about to leave. / The meeting is due to start at 10.
U hozir ketmoqchi. / Yig'ilish 10 da boshlanishi belgilangan.
The President is to visit tomorrow.
S + be bound/sure/certain to + V1; S + be likely/unlikely to + V1
He is bound to succeed. / They are likely to win the match.
U albatta muvaffaqiyatga erishadi. / Ular o'yinda yutishi ehtimol.
presentation: What are you going to do after IELTS 4.0?
I'm going to apply for a scholarship abroad.
Are you meeting anyone about a job?
Yes, I'm meeting a recruiter on Friday.
When does the interview start?

Is the new office due to open soon?
It's due to open in September.
Is Mbappé to sign a new contract?

Is he bound to score in the final?
He's bound to try — and he's likely to succeed.
Are working hours likely to get longer?
Unfortunately, they are likely to; burnout is bound to increase.
What is the company about to announce?
It's about to announce a four-day week.
Is unemployment likely to fall next year?
It's unlikely to fall quickly.
When are you starting your new job?
I'm starting on Monday — the contract says I'm to report at 9.
notes: will — o'sha paytdagi qaror/va'da/bashorat; be going to — oldindan reja; Present Continuous — kelishilgan (vaqt/joy aniq).
Writing Task 1 (grafik): "is expected to rise", "is projected to reach", "is likely to remain stable".
be to — yangiliklar va rasmiy hujjatlar; buyruq: "You are to be here at 8."

reading.title: Kylian Mbappé — a career that is bound to break records
text: Kylian Mbappé was born in 1998 in Bondy, a suburb of Paris. His father was a football coach and his mother a professional handball player, so his career was likely to be in sport from the start. At six he was already training with adults; at fourteen every big club in Europe was going to sign him, and Real Madrid invited him to visit — a visit he still describes as the day he understood he was to become a professional.

He chose Monaco, and at 16 became the youngest player in the club's history. In 2017 Paris Saint-Germain paid 180 million euros for him — the most expensive teenager ever. A year later, at 19, he scored in the World Cup final; only Pelé had done that younger. Journalists wrote that he was bound to become the best player in the world, and for once the journalists were right.

Mbappé's work ethic is famous. He is about to turn 28 and has never missed a training session through indiscipline. He studies his own matches for hours, and he is due to finish a business degree that he started online. In 2024 he finally joined Real Madrid — as a free agent, on his own terms, with a contract that is to run until 2029.

Off the pitch he is likely to be remembered for something else: he gives all his national-team salary to charity, and his foundation is going to send a hundred children from the Paris suburbs to university every year. "Talent gets you noticed," he says. "Work is what is going to keep you there."

intro: VAQT: in the morning, at the moment, before lunch, after the match. JOY: at school, in the city centre, on the roof, on the court.
TARZ: with great care, in a hurry, like a professional, by hand. SABAB: because of + ot, due to + ot, thanks to + ot.
MAQSAD: in order to + V1, so as to + V1, for + ot (for better results). TAKRORLIK: every week, once in a while, twice a day.
DARAJA: to a great extent, almost entirely, to some degree. SHART: in case of fire, under pressure, in the event of…
YON BERISH: despite / in spite of + ot/V-ing (despite the difficulty, despite being injured).
Joy: odatda gap oxirida (tarz → joy → vaqt); boshida vergul bilan urg'u.
formulas: in the morning, at the moment, before lunch / at school, in the city centre, on the roof
He trains in the morning at the club.
with great care, in a hurry, like a professional
because of / due to + ot; in order to + V1 / for + ot
He retired due to illness. / He trains in order to win.
U kasallik sababli sportni tark etdi. / U yutish uchun mashq qiladi.
every week, once in a while; to a great extent, almost entirely
Diet decides results to a great extent.
in case of + ot, under pressure
In case of injury, stop immediately.
presentation: When does Djokovic train?
In the morning, before breakfast, every single day.
Where does he prepare?
On the court and in the gym in Belgrade.
How does he eat?
With great care — a gluten-free, plant-based diet.
Why did he miss the 2022 Australian Open?
Because of his vaccine decision, he was deported.
Why does he stretch for an hour?
In order to prevent injury.
How often do you see a doctor?
Once a year, for a check-up.
To what extent does sleep affect health?
To a great extent — almost entirely, some doctors say.
What should you do in case of a heart attack?
In case of a heart attack, call an ambulance immediately.
Did he win despite the injury?
Yes, despite a torn muscle, he won the final.
How do people live longer?
Thanks to better healthcare and, to some degree, better diets.
notes: because of / due to / thanks to + OT (because + gap); despite / in spite of + OT yoki V-ing (although + gap).
in order to + V1; "for + V-ing" — maqsad emas, vazifa.
Tartib: tarz → joy → vaqt: "He trained hard in Belgrade yesterday."

reading.title: Novak Djokovic — winning against all odds, with great care
text: Novak Djokovic was born in 1987 in Belgrade, Serbia. As a child he practised on a tennis court in the mountains, and during the NATO bombing of 1999 he trained in an empty swimming pool in order to avoid the planes. Despite the war, he never missed a day. At 20 he won his first Grand Slam, in Australia, in 2008.

For years he was the third man behind Federer and Nadal, mainly because of his stamina: in long matches he collapsed, almost entirely due to breathing problems. In 2010 a doctor discovered a gluten intolerance almost by chance. Djokovic changed his nutrition with great care — no gluten, no dairy, no sugar — and within a year he became world number one. He has held that position for more than 400 weeks, a record, and he has won 24 Grand Slams, more than any man in history.

His lifestyle is famous for its discipline. He wakes at dawn, drinks warm water, stretches for an hour for the sake of injury prevention, and meditates in order to stay calm under pressure. In case of a bad day, he says, the routine saves him. Thanks to this, at 37 he was still winning — Olympic gold in Paris in 2024.

He is also controversial: in 2022 he was deported from Australia because of his refusal to be vaccinated, and many fans turned against him. He returned a year later and won the tournament. "Resilience," he says, "is built in the long run, on the days nobody sees."

intro: BE ALLOWED TO + V1 — ruxsat berilgan (og'zaki, umumiy): "He is allowed to stay out late." Inkor: isn't allowed to (taqiq).
BE PERMITTED TO + V1 — rasmiy ruxsat (qoida, hujjat): "They were permitted to enter." Rasmiy e'lonlarda: "Smoking is not permitted."
BE SUPPOSED TO + V1 — kutilgan, qoida bo'yicha shunday bo'lishi kerak: "You are supposed to wear a uniform." O'tganda — bo'lmagan: "I was supposed to call you (lekin qilmadim)."

reading.title: Nelson Mandela — the prisoner who was supposed to die in jail
text: Nelson Mandela was born in 1918 in a village in South Africa. Under the system called apartheid, black South Africans were not allowed to vote, were not permitted to live in white areas and were supposed to carry a pass at all times. Mandela, a young lawyer in Johannesburg, joined the African National Congress and organised protests. When the ANC was banned, he went underground; in 1962 he was arrested, and in 1964 he was sentenced to life imprisonment.

On Robben Island prisoners were permitted one letter and one visitor every six months. They were supposed to break rocks all day and were not allowed to talk while working. Mandela was expected to be forgotten. Instead, he studied law by correspondence, taught other prisoners and, after twenty years, was allowed to negotiate with the government — from his cell.

In 1990 he was released. Everyone was afraid of civil war: he was supposed to want revenge after 27 years. He chose reconciliation. In 1994, in the first election in which every citizen was allowed to vote, he became president. At his inauguration his former jailers were permitted to sit as guests of honour. A truth commission allowed victims and criminals to speak instead of fighting.

Mandela served only one term — he was allowed to stay, but he refused — and died in 2013. His autobiography, "Long Walk to Freedom", ends with a sentence every IELTS student ought to remember: "To be free is not merely to cast off one's chains, but to live in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others."

intro: THE — aniq, ma'lum narsa: ikkinchi marta ("I saw a man. The man was tall"); yagona (the sun, the moon, the internet, the government); superlativ/tartib (the biggest, the first, the same, the only).

GEOGRAFIYA — THE bilan: daryolar (the Amu Darya), dengiz/okean (the Aral Sea, the Pacific), tog' tizmalari (the Tian Shan, the Alps), cho'llar (the Kyzylkum), orollar guruhi (the Maldives), qutblar (the North Pole), "United/Republic/Kingdom/States" davlatlar (the UK, the USA, the Czech Republic), ko'plik davlatlar (the Netherlands, the Philippines).

THE'siz: davlatlar (Uzbekistan, France), shaharlar (Tashkent), ko'llar (Lake Baikal), cho'qqilar (Mount Everest), qit'alar (Asia), ko'chalar (Navoi Street), tillar (English), umumiy ma'no (Life is hard; Cities are noisy), ovqat/oy/kun (at lunch, in May, on Monday), vazifa ma'nosida (go to school/hospital/prison/bed).

reading.title: Mahmud Kashgari — the man who drew the first map of the Turkic world
text: Mahmud Kashgari was born around 1029 near Kashgar, a city on the Silk Road in the east of the Karakhanid state, which ruled the lands from the Syr Darya to the Tian Shan. He came from the ruling family, but a palace struggle forced him to leave. For fifteen years he travelled through the steppes, the deserts and the mountain valleys of Central Asia, living with the tribes and writing down their words.

In the 1070s, in Baghdad, he finished "Diwan Lughat al-Turk" — the first dictionary of the Turkic languages. It contains about 7,500 words, with examples from poems, proverbs and songs, and it records the dialects of dozens of tribes, from the Caspian Sea to China. Nobody before him had treated Turkic as a language worth studying next to Arabic.

The book also contains something unique: the first world map made by a Turk. It is circular, and at the centre is not Mecca or Baghdad but Balasagun, the Karakhanid capital in the Chu Valley. Around it are the cities of the Silk Road — Kashgar, Samarkand, Bukhara — the rivers, the deserts and the mountains, drawn with colours: green for seas, red for mountains, yellow for sand.

The manuscript was lost for eight centuries and found in Istanbul in 1914. Today Kashgari is honoured in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkey and China, and his map is the first picture we have of the geography of the Turkic peoples — the cities, the rivers and the steppes that are still ours.

lessons.title: Had better, Would rather, Prefer
lessons.grammar_topic: HAD BETTER (tavsiya/ogohlantirish) / WOULD RATHER (afzal ko'rish — hozir) / PREFER (umumiy afzallik) + would rather + S + Past Simple
lessons.vocab_topic: Essential Words 8 — Media, music and entertainment (media, musiqa, ko'ngilochar soha)
lessons.book_ref: Student's book IELTS 4.0: Lesson 8 – Had better, would rather, prefer (3 qatorli jadval); Essential Words 8; Speaking sample: Music; Audio 41–45 (ustoz skripti); Reading — Taylor Swift (Jony Academy matni).
objectives: had better (tavsiya, kuchli) / would rather (hozirgi tanlov) / prefer (umumiy odat) ni to'g'ri qolipda ishlatish.
Inkor shakllar: had better not, would rather not, prefer not to.
would rather + boshqa ega + Past Simple (I'd rather you came early); prefer … to … / rather than.
Media va musiqa Essential Words 8 bilan Speaking "Music" mavzusi va media ta'siri haqida gapirish.
materials: Essential Words 8 — Media, music and entertainment (media, musiqa, ko'ngilochar soha) CORE 20 varag'i.
timeline: Ustoz: "You'd better switch off your phone (ogohlantirish). I'd rather listen to music than talk (hozirgi tanlov). I prefer live concerts to streaming (umumiy)." — uch ma'no, uch qolip.
20 savol, 15 soniya; oldingi dars lug'ati + grammatikasi.

Kitob jadvali: had better + V1 (yaxshisi… — tavsiya/ogohlantirish, aks holda muammo); would rather + V1 (+ than + V1) (afzal ko'raman — hozirgi/aniq tanlov); prefer + ot/V-ing + to + ot/V-ing (umumiy afzallik) / prefer + to V1 + rather than + V1. Qo'shimcha: would rather + boshqa ega + Past Simple ("I'd rather you didn't smoke"), had better not.
Essential Words 8 — Media, music and entertainment (media, musiqa, ko'ngilochar soha) — CORE 20
Har so'z bilan yangi grammatika qolipida gap.
Kitob: formula → gap → tarjima; warm-up / normativ / coin me'yorlari.
Sinf matni + 3 topshiriq; kitob Topic'lari uyga.
Ko'p uchragan xatolar doskada; STRONG lug'at kuchlilarga.

intro: HAD BETTER + V1 — "yaxshisi …, aks holda …" — kuchli tavsiya/ogohlantirish (hozir/yaqin kelajak): "You had better go now." Qisqa: 'd better; inkor: had better not.
WOULD RATHER + V1 — "afzal ko'raman" (aniq holat, hozir): "I would rather stay home tonight." + than + V1: "I'd rather read than watch TV." Inkor: would rather not.
WOULD RATHER + boshqa ega + PAST SIMPLE — boshqa odam qilishini xohlash: "I'd rather you didn't post that." (hozir haqida).

PREFER — umumiy afzallik: prefer + ot/V-ing + to + ot/V-ing ("I prefer reading to watching TV"); prefer + to V1 + rather than + V1 ("I prefer to listen rather than talk"). would prefer to — aniq holat, muloyim.
formulas: You had better go now. / You'd better not be late.
Yaxshisi hozir ketsang bo'ladi. / Kech qolmaganing ma'qul.
S + would rather (+ not) + V1 (+ than + V1)
I would rather stay home tonight. / I'd rather read than watch TV.
Bugun uyda qolishni afzal ko'raman. / TV ko'rishdan ko'ra o'qishni afzal ko'raman.
S + would rather + S2 + Past Simple
I'd rather you didn't post that photo.
She prefers tea to coffee. / I prefer reading to watching TV.
U choyni qahvadan afzal ko'radi. / O'qishni TV ko'rishdan afzal ko'raman.
S + prefer + to V1 + rather than + V1
I prefer to stream music rather than buy CDs.
Disk sotib olishdan ko'ra musiqani striming qilishni afzal ko'raman.
S + would prefer + to V1 (muloyim, aniq holat)
I'd prefer to sit near the stage.
presentation: Would you rather go to a concert or watch it online?
I'd rather go to the concert — nothing beats live music.
Do you prefer pop to classical?
I prefer pop to classical, but I'd rather not listen to it all day.
Hadn't we better buy the tickets now?
Yes, we'd better buy them today; they'll sell out.
Would you rather I didn't play music while you study?
I'd rather you turned it down a little.
Do you prefer streaming or CDs?
I prefer streaming to CDs — it's cheaper.
Had Taylor Swift better re-record her albums?
She'd better — and she did, to own her music.
Would you rather read the news or watch it?
I'd rather read it than watch it; TV news is too dramatic.
Do you prefer to listen to music alone rather than with friends?
I prefer to listen alone; friends talk too much.
Hadn't you better check the source before sharing?
Yes, I'd better check it — fake news spreads fast.
Would you rather be famous or rich?
I'd rather be rich; fame ruins privacy.

would rather + V1 (to yo'q); prefer + to V1 yoki V-ing.
"would rather + S2 + Past Simple" — hozir/kelajak; o'tgan afsus: would rather + S2 + Past Perfect.

reading.title: Taylor Swift — she'd rather own her music than be owned by it
text: Taylor Swift was born in 1989 in Pennsylvania. At 14 she told her parents that she would rather write songs in Nashville than stay at school in the suburbs, and the family moved. Her first album, country music written entirely by a teenager, came out in 2006. Record labels had told her she'd better wait until she was older; she preferred not to.

By 2015 she was the biggest pop star in the world. Then, in 2019, her old record label was sold, and with it the master recordings of her first six albums. Swift had asked to buy them herself; the label preferred to sell to someone else. Most artists would have accepted this. Swift did something unprecedented: she re-recorded all six albums as "Taylor's Versions", so that fans would rather stream her copies than the originals. It worked — the new versions topped the charts, and the old masters lost their value.

Her Eras Tour (2023–24) became the first tour in history to earn more than two billion dollars; economists measured its impact on the cities it visited, and Time magazine named her Person of the Year. Her fans, the Swifties, are famous for preferring vinyl records and stadium tickets to streaming.

Swift writes all her own songs, and most are autobiographical. "You'd better write your own story," she told students at New York University, "because if you don't, someone else will — and they'll get the copyright." Journalists would rather write about her boyfriends; she would rather they wrote about her songwriting.

reading.title: Ruslan Chagaev — the night Uzbekistan saw a giant fall
text: Ruslan Chagaev was born in 1978 in Andijan. As a boy he watched his older brothers box in a small gym, and by 19 he had become an amateur world champion. He fought for Uzbekistan at the 2000 Olympics, and everyone expected to see him win a medal; instead they saw him lose early and, soon after, turn professional in Germany.

For seven years nobody saw him lose. Then, in April 2007, in Stuttgart, he faced Nikolay Valuev — the WBA heavyweight champion, a seven-foot giant weighing 145 kg who had never been beaten in 46 fights. Chagaev was 1.85 m and 30 kg lighter. Millions of Uzbeks stayed up until 3 a.m. to watch him fight. In the fourth round they saw him land a left hand that shook the giant; in the twelfth they heard the final bell ring and watched the judges give a majority decision — to Chagaev. Uzbekistan had its first world heavyweight champion, and Andijan saw its streets fill with people at dawn.

His career was never simple. Doctors had seen him fighting hepatitis B for years, and a suspension kept him out of the ring for months. He lost the belt in 2009, but in 2014, at 35, fans watched him make a comeback and win the WBA title again. He retired in 2019 with 34 wins.

Today young boxers in Andijan can be seen training in a gym that carries his name. "I saw my brothers fight and I copied them," he says. "Now I want children to see us and copy us — that's how a sport lives."

reading.title: Rihanna — the one who found a gap in the beauty market
text: Robyn Rihanna Fenty was born in 1988 in Barbados, a small island in the Caribbean. At 16 she sang for an American producer who was on holiday there; he was the one who took her to New York. Within two years she had a number-one single, and by 2012 she was one of the biggest pop stars in the world.

Most stars sell perfume with their name on it. Rihanna wanted something else. She had noticed that makeup brands made foundation in ten or fifteen shades — and none of them were the ones that matched dark skin. Millions of women had the same problem: they could see products everywhere, but never the one made for them. In 2017 she launched Fenty Beauty with 40 shades on the first day. The darkest ones sold out within hours. Other brands copied her within a year; the industry called it "the Fenty effect".

She kept a 50% stake in the company — the one decision that made her a billionaire in 2021, richer than any other musician. Her lingerie brand, Savage X Fenty, uses models of every size and colour, because, she says, "everyone wants to see one like themselves."

In 2021 Barbados became a republic, and Rihanna was named a national hero at the ceremony. She has not released an album since 2016; asked why, she smiled: "I'd rather build the ones that last than another one that plays for three minutes."

intro: CLEFT (It-cleft): It + is/was + TA'KID + that/who + qolgan gap. "It was Marie Curie who discovered radium." (kim); "It was in 1898 that she discovered it." (qachon); "It is honesty that matters most." (nima).
WHAT-CLAUSE (Wh-cleft): What + ega + fe'l + is/was + TA'KID. "What I need is a break." / "What she discovered was a new element." Boshqa: "All I want is…", "The only thing that matters is…".
EMPHATIC DO: do/does/did + V1 — fe'lga urg'u (haqiqatan, rostdan). "I do like this movie!" / "She did finish her work." Buyruqda: "Do sit down."

FRONTING: ob'ekt yoki holat gap boshiga: "This book, I really enjoyed." / "In Paris she found her laboratory." Inkor so'z bilan — inversiya: "Never had a woman won a Nobel Prize before." / "Not only did she win one, but she won two."
formulas: It was John who broke the window.
It is honesty that matters most. / It was in 1898 that radium was discovered.
Eng muhimi — halollik. / Radiy aynan 1898-da kashf etilgan.
What I need is a break. / What he said was shocking.
Menga kerak narsa — dam olish. / U aytgan narsa hayratlanarli edi.
I do like this movie! / She did finish her work.
Men bu filmni rostdan yoqtiraman! / U ishini haqiqatan tugatdi.
This book, I really enjoyed. / In Paris she began her research.
Bu kitobni men rostdan yoqtirdim. / Parijda u tadqiqotini boshladi.
Never / Not only / Rarely + yordamchi + S + V
Never had a woman won a Nobel Prize. / Not only did she win one, but two.
Ilgari hech bir ayol Nobel mukofotini olmagan edi. / U nafaqat bitta, balki ikkita oldi.
presentation: Who discovered radium?

notes: It-cleft: shaxs → who yoki that; narsa/vaqt/joy → that. "It was yesterday that…" (when emas).
What-clause dan keyin fe'l birlikda (What I need IS…); ta'kid ot yoki to-infinitive bo'lishi mumkin ("What I want is to rest").
Emphatic do — faqat Present/Past Simple da; boshqa zamonda urg'u ohang bilan.

reading.title: Marie Curie — it was a woman in a leaking shed who changed science
text: Maria Skłodowska was born in 1867 in Warsaw, when Poland was ruled by Russia and women were not allowed to go to university. What she did for six years was work as a governess to pay for her sister's studies in Paris; then her sister paid for hers. It was in 1891 that she arrived at the Sorbonne, so poor that she sometimes fainted from hunger during lectures. She finished first in her physics class.

In Paris she met Pierre Curie, and they married in 1895. What caught her attention was a strange discovery: uranium gave off invisible rays. She wanted to know why. In a leaking wooden shed that the university gave them, she boiled tonnes of pitchblende ore, stirring it with an iron rod "almost as big as myself". It was in 1898 that she found two new elements — polonium, named after her homeland, and radium, which glowed in the dark. She did not just find them; she invented the word for what they did: radioactivity.

Never had a woman won a Nobel Prize before 1903, when she shared the physics prize with Pierre. Pierre died in 1906, and it was Marie who took his post — the first female professor at the Sorbonne. In 1911 she won a second Nobel, in chemistry. Nobody had ever won two in different sciences; nobody has done it since.

What she refused to do was patent radium. "It belongs to everyone," she said. In World War I she built mobile X-ray units, drove them to the front herself and helped a million wounded soldiers. The radiation that made her famous killed her in 1934. Her notebooks are still radioactive today and are kept in a lead-lined box. What she left behind was more than two elements: it was proof that curiosity, not permission, is what makes a scientist.

reading.title: Muhammad Yunus — the smaller the loan, the bigger the change
text: Muhammad Yunus was born in 1940 in Chittagong, Bangladesh. He studied economics in the United States and came home to teach it at a university. Then, in 1974, famine came to Bangladesh, and he found that the more theories he taught in the classroom, the less they explained the hunger outside the window. So he walked into the nearest village.

There he met a woman who made bamboo stools. She had to borrow money from a moneylender to buy bamboo, and the moneylender took nearly all her profit: the more she worked, the poorer she stayed. Yunus found 42 people in the village in the same trap. The total they needed was 27 dollars. He lent it from his own pocket, and every cent was repaid.

Banks refused to lend to the poor because they had no collateral. Yunus argued the opposite: the poorer people are, the more carefully they repay, because a loan is their only chance. In 1983 he founded Grameen Bank — "the village bank". It lends tiny sums, with no collateral, to groups of five who support one another; 97 per cent of the borrowers are women, because the more money women control, the more of it reaches the children. The repayment rate is higher than at most ordinary banks. Today the bank has nine million borrowers, and the idea — microcredit — has been copied in more than a hundred countries.

In 2006 Yunus and Grameen Bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize. In 2024, at 84, he was asked to lead Bangladesh's interim government after student protests. His dream is unchanged: "The sooner we put poverty in a museum, the better. The poor are not the problem — they are the solution."

intro: EVEN — "hatto": ta'kid, kutilmagan holat: "Even he didn't know the answer." (hatto u ham). EVEN THOUGH + haqiqat (garchi… bo'lsa ham): "She smiled even though she was tired." EVEN IF + faraz (agar … bo'lsa ham): "I'll go even if it rains."

IN CASE — "ehtimol … bo'lib qolar deb, ehtiyot uchun": harakat OLDINDAN qilinadi: "Take an umbrella in case it rains." (yomg'ir yog'ishi mumkin deb — hozir ol). Taqqoslang: "Take an umbrella if it rains" (yog'sa — keyin ol). IN CASE OF + ot (ogohlantirish yozuvlarida): "In case of fire, use the stairs."
AS LONG AS — "faqat … bo'lsa, … sharti bilan": "You can stay as long as you're quiet."
PROVIDED (THAT) — rasmiy/yozma shart: "You can go out provided that you finish your work." PROVIDING (THAT) — xuddi shu, og'zaki: "Providing you have a ticket, you can enter."
Bu shart bog'lovchilaridan keyin kelasi zamon EMAS, Present Simple: "as long as you ARE quiet", "provided you FINISH".
formulas: Even he didn't know the answer.
S + V + even though + HAQIQAT / even if + FARAZ
She smiled even though she was tired. / I'll travel even if it's expensive.
U charchagan bo'lsa ham jilmaydi. / Qimmat bo'lsa ham sayohat qilaman.
Take an umbrella in case it rains.
Yomg'ir yog'ib qolsa deb, soyabon ol.
S + V + as long as + S + V (Present)
You can stay as long as you're quiet.
You can go out provided that you finish work. / Providing you have a ticket, you can enter.
Ishni tugatsang, chiqishing mumkin. / Chiptang bo'lsa, kirishing mumkin.
presentation: Did Ibn Battuta know the languages?

reading.title: Ibn Battuta — the man who never travelled the same road twice
text: In 1325 a 21-year-old law student left Tangier, in Morocco, to make the hajj to Mecca. He planned to be away for about a year. He came home 29 years later, having travelled 120,000 kilometres — three times farther than Marco Polo — even though he never had a map. His name was Ibn Battuta.

He crossed North Africa with caravans, in case bandits attacked lone travellers, and reached Mecca in 1326. Then, instead of going home, he made a rule: never travel the same road twice as long as another road existed. He went on to Iraq and Persia, sailed down the coast of East Africa, and crossed Anatolia and the Golden Horde in a winter so cold that, he wrote, he had to wear three fur coats even to pray. In 1333 he reached Khwarazm and praised Urgench as one of the finest cities he had seen — and he had seen Cairo and Damascus. From there he visited Bukhara and Samarkand, "one of the largest and most beautiful cities in the world", before crossing the Hindu Kush to India.

In Delhi the Sultan made him a judge and paid him well, provided that he stayed. He stayed eight years, even though the Sultan was famous for executing people he disliked. Then he was sent as an ambassador to China; he was shipwrecked, robbed, and reached the Maldives with nothing — where he was made a judge again, providing he married locally. He did, four times.

He returned to Damascus in 1348 in case his family had survived the Black Death, which was killing thousands a day; his father was dead. He finally went home in 1349, then set out again — across the Sahara to the Mali Empire — at nearly 50. Back in Morocco, he dictated everything to a scholar, and the book, the Rihla, survives today. Even now, scholars use it as the best record of the 14th-century Muslim world, from Uzbekistan to Zanzibar.

intro: ANAPHORIC reference — OLDIN aytilgan narsaga ishora: "Tom bought a car. He loves it." (He = Tom, it = car). Eng ko'p uchraydi: he/she/it/they, this/that, the + ot.
CATAPHORIC (qo'shimcha) — KEYIN aytiladigan narsaga: "When he arrived, Tom sat down." (he = Tom).
EXOPHORIC — matndan TASHQARIDAGI vaziyatga: "Look at that!" (osmonga ishora qilib); "Pass me that."
COMPARATIVE — taqqoslash orqali bog'lash: "My house is bigger than hers." (hers = her house); "the same", "other", "such".
SUBSTITUTION — iborani boshqa so'z bilan ALMASHTIRISH: "I like apples. So do I." (so do I = I like apples); "one/ones" ("a red one"); "do so"; "I think so / I hope not".
ELLIPSIS — so'zni TUSHIRIB qoldirish: "She likes tea. I don't (like tea)." / "Can you come? — I can (come)."
DEMONSTRATIVES — this/that/these/those: "I like this book. That one is boring." Yozma matnda "this" = hozirgina aytilgan fikr: "Prices rose. This surprised everyone."
formulas: Tom bought a car. He loves it.
Tom mashina sotib oldi. U uni yaxshi ko'radi.
comparative + than + hers/mine/the other; the same/such
My house is bigger than hers.
So do I / Neither do I / one, ones / do so
I like apples. So do I. / I need a pen — a blue one.
Men olmani yaxshi ko'raman. Men ham. / Menga ruchka kerak — ko'ki.
She likes tea. I don't. / Can you come? — I can.
U choyni yaxshi ko'radi. Men esa yo'q. / Kela olasanmi? — Ha.
I like this book. That one is boring. / Prices rose. This surprised everyone.
Bu kitob yoqadi. Unisi zerikarli. / Narxlar oshdi. Bu hammani hayratga soldi.
presentation: "Zamakhshari wrote a dictionary. It is still used." — what is "it"?
"It" refers to the dictionary — anaphoric.

reading.title: Mahmud az-Zamakhshari — the Khwarazmian who taught the Arabs their own language
text: In 1075 a boy was born in Zamakhshar, a small village near Urgench in Khwarazm. His name was Mahmud, and the village gave him the name the world remembers: az-Zamakhshari. His father was a poor imam, but he sent the boy to Bukhara to study. There Mahmud lost a leg in a snowstorm; for the rest of his life he walked on a wooden one, and he carried a letter from witnesses in case anyone thought it was a punishment.

His mother tongue was Persian, and he grew up hearing Khwarazmian and Turkic in the streets. Arabic was his fourth language. Yet it was Arabic he mastered best. In his forties he travelled to Mecca and lived beside the Kaaba for years; this earned him the title Jar Allah, "God's neighbour". There he wrote Al-Mufassal, a grammar of Arabic so clear that Arab scholars themselves taught it for five centuries. "A non-Arab has explained our language to us," one of them admitted. Such praise was rare.

His most famous book is Al-Kashshaf, a commentary on the Quran that explains the meaning of every verse through language and rhetoric. Scholars who disliked his theology still used it; they had no better one. He also wrote Asas al-Balagha, the first dictionary to separate literal meanings from metaphors, and Muqaddimat al-Adab, a dictionary of Arabic with Persian, Khwarazmian and Turkic translations. The latter is priceless today: the Khwarazmian language is extinct, and his book is one of the few records of it.

He returned home and died in Gurganj — now Urgench — in 1144. His tomb is still there. Nine centuries later UNESCO marked his anniversary, and linguists still open his dictionaries. This is the strange fate of a man who lost a leg but never lost a word.

intro: LINKING VERB — ega bilan uning HOLATini bog'laydi; keyin SIFAT (ravish emas): "She is happy." / "He seems tired." / "The soup tastes delicious."
HOLAT: be (is happy), seem (seems tired), appear (appears nervous), remain (remained calm), stay (stayed silent).
SEZGI: feel (I feel cold), look (You look great), sound (That sounds interesting), taste (tastes delicious), smell (smell nice).
O'ZGARISH: become (became friends), get (getting dark), grow (grew angry), turn (turned pale). become + ot ham mumkin (became a doctor); get/grow/turn odatda + sifat.
FARQ: "She looked sad" (holat — sifat) vs "She looked at me sadly" (harakat — ravish). "The flowers smell sweet" vs "He smelled the flowers carefully".
+ OT bilan: look like / sound like / feel like + ot ("It sounds like a good idea"); seem/appear + to be ("He seems to be ill"); It seems that….

reading.title: Billie Eilish — she looked nothing like a pop star, and that became the point
text: Billie Eilish was born in Los Angeles in 2001 and was home-schooled by two actor parents who never became rich. At 13 she recorded a song called "Ocean Eyes" with her brother Finneas in his bedroom. It sounded like nothing else — a whisper over a slow beat — and within a year millions had heard it. By 17 she seemed to be everywhere; by 18 she had become the youngest artist ever to win the four main Grammy awards in one night.

She looked wrong for pop, and that was deliberate. She wore baggy clothes so that her body stayed her own business, dyed her hair green and black, and sang about nightmares, sleep paralysis and death. Teenagers felt understood. "I felt so lonely at 14," she said later, "and I wanted someone to sound the way I felt."

Fame did not feel the way it looks. She has Tourette syndrome — small tics that get worse when she is tired — and she grew depressed as the tours got longer. At 15 she had suicidal thoughts. She has been open about all of it: the therapy, the body-image problems, the panic attacks before shows. Her honesty seemed shocking at first, then it became normal, and mental health turned from a secret into a topic that stars are expected to talk about.

Her music kept growing. "Happier Than Ever" starts soft and turns furious; her theme for a James Bond film won an Oscar; and "What Was I Made For?", written for the Barbie film, won a second, making her the youngest person ever with two Oscars at 22. Her tours stay plastic-free, and she remains a loud climate activist. "I looked strange and felt terrible," she told an interviewer, "and it still turned out fine. That's the message."

intro: BACKSHIFT — reporting fe'l o'tgan zamonda (said, told) bo'lsa, ichki gap bir qadam ORQAGA: Present Simple → Past Simple; Present Continuous → Past Continuous; Present Perfect → Past Perfect; Past Simple → Past Perfect; Past Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous.
MODALLAR: will → would; can → could; may → might; must → had to; should/could/might/would — o'zgarmaydi.
OLMOSH: "I" → he/she; "we" → they; "my" → his/her; "you" → me/us (kim bilan gaplashganiga qarab).

VAQT/JOY: now → then; today → that day; yesterday → the day before; tomorrow → the next/following day; last week → the week before; next year → the following year; here → there; this → that; ago → before.
SAY vs TELL: said (that) + gap; told + KIMGA + (that) + gap. "He said he was tired." / "He told me he was tired."
Umumiy haqiqat va hozir ham to'g'ri gap — backshift shart emas: "She said the Earth goes round the Sun."
formulas: He said, "I work hard." → He said he worked hard.
She said, "I am studying." → She said she was studying.
Present Perfect / Past Simple → Past Perfect
"We have finished." → They said they had finished. / "I lost my key." → I said I had lost my key.
Ular tugatganini aytishdi. / Kalitimni yo'qotganimni aytdim.
S + said + S + had been + V-ing
"I was watching TV." → He said he had been watching TV.
will / can / may → would / could / might
"I will call you." → She said she would call me. / "I can swim." → He said he could swim. / "I may come." → She said she might come.
U menga qo'ng'iroq qilishini aytdi. / U suza olishini aytdi. / U kelishi mumkinligini aytdi.
S + told + OB'EKT + (that) + gap; now → then, tomorrow → the next day
"I'll see you here tomorrow." → She told me she would see me there the next day.
U meni ertasi kuni o'sha yerda ko'rishini aytdi.

reading.title: Zulfiya — the poet who said she would not weep
text: Zulfiya Isroilova was born in 1915 in Degrez, a mahalla of craftsmen in old Tashkent. Her father cast iron pots; her mother sang. Years later Zulfiya said that her mother's lullabies had been her first poetry, and that her father had made her first notebook with his own hands. She published her first poems at 17 and told a friend that she would write for the women of Uzbekistan, because nobody else was.

In 1935 she married the poet Hamid Olimjon. They had two children, and she said later that those nine years had been the happiest of her life. Then, in July 1944, Hamid Olimjon was killed in a car accident. Zulfiya was 29. Relatives told her she should remarry; she said she would raise the children alone, and she did. Her daughter Hulkar remembered that her mother had written every night after the housework was finished, and that she had never once cried in front of them. "I will not weep," one of her most famous poems begins, "because my children are watching."

Grief made her famous, but she refused to stay in it. She edited the women's magazine "Saodat" for thirty years, translated Pushkin and Lesya Ukrainka into Uzbek, and travelled to India, Egypt and Japan as a poet of the East. Readers said that she wrote like a mother and a soldier at the same time.

She died in 1996. In 1999 Uzbekistan created the Zulfiya State Prize for gifted girls, and in 2004 she was named a Hero of Uzbekistan. Her granddaughter said recently that the family still kept the iron pot her father had made — and the notebook. "She told us," the granddaughter said, "that a family is not the people who live in the house. It is the people you refuse to forget."

reading.title: Imam al-Bukhari — the boy from Bukhara who asked whether every story was true
text: Muhammad ibn Ismail was born in Bukhara in 810. His father died when he was a baby, and as a small child he lost his sight; his mother later said that she had prayed every night until it returned. By ten he was memorising hadiths — reports of what the Prophet had said and done — and by sixteen he had left for Mecca with his mother and brother. He did not come home for sixteen years.

In every city — Mecca, Medina, Baghdad, Damascus, Cairo — he did the same thing. He listened to a scholar, and then he asked questions. He asked who had told the scholar the story, and who had told that person, and whether each of them had actually met. He asked whether the narrator had been known for honesty, and if his memory had been reliable in old age. If one link in the chain was weak, he rejected the report. In this way he examined about 600,000 reports and kept around 7,000. The book he made from them, Sahih al-Bukhari, is still considered the most authentic collection in the Muslim world.

Scholars in Baghdad once tested him. Ten men each read him ten hadiths with the chains deliberately mixed up. They asked him whether he recognised them. He said he did not — and then he repeated all one hundred, correcting every error from memory. Nobody asked him again.

Back in Bukhara, the governor asked whether the imam would teach his sons privately at the palace. Bukhari asked why the governor's sons should not sit with everyone else. For that answer he was sent into exile, and he died in 870 in Khartank, a village near Samarkand. His mausoleum there is now one of the largest memorial complexes in Uzbekistan. Historians say that his method — ask who said it, ask how they knew — was a scientific method centuries before the word existed.

intro: BUYRUQ → told / ordered + KIMGA + TO + V1: "Open the window." → He told me to open the window.
TAQIQ → told / warned + KIMGA + NOT TO + V1: "Don't shout." → She told me not to shout. / "Don't touch it, it's hot!" → He warned me not to touch it.
ILTIMOS → asked / requested / begged + KIMGA + TO + V1: "Please sit down." → The teacher asked us to sit down.
MASLAHAT → advised / recommended + KIMGA + TO + V1: "You should drink water." → He advised me to drink water.
TAKLIF → suggested + V-ING (ob'ektsiz!): "Let's take a break." → She suggested taking a break. Yoki suggested (that) we (should) take a break.

reading.title: Pep Guardiola — the coach who told Messi to play in the wrong position
text: Josep "Pep" Guardiola was born in 1971 in Santpedor, a village in Catalonia. His father was a bricklayer who told him to finish everything he started. At 13 he joined La Masia, Barcelona's academy, where the coaches told every boy to control the ball before he did anything else. Johan Cruyff, the club's manager, saw the thin teenager and told him to play with his head, not his legs. Guardiola became the midfielder around whom Cruyff's "Dream Team" was built.

In 2008 Barcelona asked him to manage the first team. He was 37 and had coached only the reserves. In his first meeting he told the players to run more than any opponent, warned them not to keep the ball for the sake of it, and asked them to pass fifteen times before shooting. Then, before a match against Real Madrid in 2009, he told Lionel Messi — a winger — to play in the centre as a "false nine". Barcelona won 6–2. That year the club won six trophies, something no team had ever done; journalists asked him to explain his system, and he refused to use the word tiki-taka, which he said meant "passing with no purpose".

He left in 2012, telling the club he needed a sabbatical. Bayern Munich asked him to bring his ideas to Germany; Manchester City then asked him to do the same in England, and in 2023 the club won the treble, including its first Champions League. Players describe him as obsessive: he reminded them to watch match videos even on holiday, and once advised a defender to move into midfield when the team had the ball — the "inverted full-back", now copied everywhere.
Asked what leadership meant, he pointed to Cruyff. "He told me to win," Guardiola said, "but he told me to play well first. Everything I ask my players to do comes from that sentence."

intro: PHRASAL VERB = fe'l + zarracha (up, after, into…); ma'no ko'pincha so'zma-so'z emas: look up to = hurmat qilmoq.
LOOK AFTER (qaramoq, g'amxo'rlik) / LOOK FOR (qidirmoq) / LOOK INTO (tekshirmoq) — ajralmaydi, ob'ekt zarrachadan keyin: "look after her brother", "look into the case".
LOOK UP (lug'atdan qidirmoq) / LOOK OVER (ko'zdan kechirmoq) — ajraladi: "look up the word" = "look the word up"; olmosh bo'lsa FAQAT o'rtada: "look it up".
LOOK FORWARD TO (+ V-ing / ot), LOOK UP TO (hurmat), LOOK DOWN ON (mensimaslik) — 3 so'zli, ajralmaydi: "I look forward to seeing you."
LOOK OUT! (ehtiyot bo'l!), LOOK AROUND (aylanib ko'rmoq), LOOK BACK ON (o'tmishni eslamoq).
formulas: She looks after her little brother. / I'm looking for my keys.
U ukasiga g'amxo'rlik qiladi. / Kalitlarimni qidiryapman.
S + look forward to + V-ing / ot
We look forward to the holidays. / I look forward to seeing you.
Biz ta'tilni intiqlik bilan kutyapmiz. / Sizni ko'rishni intiqlik bilan kutaman.
S + look up + ot / look + OT/OLMOSH + up
You can look the word up in a dictionary. / Look it up.
So'zni lug'atdan qidirsang bo'ladi. / Uni qidirib ko'r.
look up to / look down on
S + look up to / down on + KIM (ajralmaydi)
I look up to my grandfather. / Don't look down on others.
Men bobomni hurmat qilaman. / Boshqalarga past nazar bilan qarama.
S + look into + ISH (tekshirmoq) / look over + HUJJAT (ko'zdan kechirmoq)
The police are looking into the case. / He looked over the report quickly.
Politsiya ishni tekshiryapti. / U hisobotni tezda ko'zdan kechirdi.
Look out! / look around + JOY / look back on + O'TMISH
Look out! There's a car coming! / Let's look around the museum. / She looked back on her childhood.
Ehtiyot bo'l! Mashina kelyapti! / Muzeyni aylanib chiqaylik. / U bolaligini esladi.

reading.title: Cho'lpon — the poet whose readers looked after his books for fifty years
text: Abdulhamid Sulaymon was born in Andijan in 1897, the son of a merchant who wrote poetry himself. The boy looked up to his father, learned Persian and Arabic at the madrasa and Russian at the Russian school, and by 17 was publishing under the name Cho'lpon — "the morning star". He looked around him and did not like what he saw: a nation without modern schools, newspapers or theatre. He joined the Jadids, the reformers who looked forward to an enlightened Uzbekistan, and wrote for their journals.

His first collection, "Uyg'onish" ("Awakening"), came out in 1922. Readers looked for the old rhymes of classical poetry and found something new: short lines, everyday words, and images — night, spring, wind, a bird — that meant more than they said. In "Go'zal", the most loved poem in the language, a man looks at a beautiful girl and looks back on everything his people have lost. Officials looked into the poem and decided that "the beautiful one" was not a girl at all, but the nation.

He looked over his shoulder for the rest of his life. His novel "Kecha va kunduz" ("Night and Day"), about a girl named Zebi who looks for love and finds a prison, was called nationalist; his translation of Hamlet was praised, then banned. In 1937 he was arrested, and on 4 October 1938 he was shot in Tashkent together with Abdulla Qodiriy and Fitrat. His books were banned for fifty years. Families looked after hidden copies, copied poems by hand, and taught them to their children in whispers.

In 1956 the state looked into his case again and cleared his name, but the books stayed locked away until 1991, when independent Uzbekistan gave him the Navoi State Prize. Today students look up "Go'zal" on their phones, and every 31 August the country looks back on the writers it lost. "My heart is a bird," he wrote. It took half a century, but the bird got out.

intro: TRANSPORT: get IN / get OUT OF — mashina, taksi (kichik); get ON / get OFF — avtobus, poyezd, samolyot, velosiped, ot (katta yoki ustiga chiqiladigan).

QIYINCHILIK: get over (kasallik, ayriliq — yengib o'tmoq), get through (qiyin davrdan o'tmoq; telefon — bog'lanmoq), get by (kam pul bilan kun ko'rmoq), get rid of (qutulmoq).

reading.title: Serena Williams — the girl from Compton who never let anything get her down
text: Before his daughters were born, Richard Williams watched a tennis final on television and saw the winner get a cheque for 40,000 dollars. He got a notebook and wrote a 78-page plan to get his future children to the top of a sport he had never played. Venus was born in 1980 and Serena in 1981. The family lived in Compton, Los Angeles, where they got by on very little money. The public courts were free, cracked and sometimes dangerous; Richard got the girls out of bed at six every morning and got them onto those courts before school.

Tennis was a white, wealthy sport, and many people expected the sisters to get nowhere. They got ahead anyway. Serena's serve became the most feared shot in the women's game, and she won her first Grand Slam at 17. The sisters got on so well off the court that they won 14 doubles titles together — and played nine Grand Slam finals against each other without ever letting the rivalry get between them.

Serena got through things that would have ended most careers. In 2003 her sister Yetunde was murdered, and the family never fully got over it. In 2001, crowds at Indian Wells booed her with racist insults; she refused to return for 14 years, then got back in 2015 to a standing ovation. In 2017 she won the Australian Open while pregnant. After her daughter was born, a blood clot nearly killed her, but she got back on court within a year.

She finished with 23 Grand Slam singles titles — more than anyone in the Open era — and four Olympic gold medals. At her last US Open in 2022, 24,000 fans got to their feet. She did not say she was retiring; she said she was "evolving". Today her investment fund, Serena Ventures, gets money to founders who are usually ignored. "People never expected me to get here," she said. "That's exactly why I did."
